contrast: Nothing to do with the everyday verb *fetch* (сходить и принести); the adjective means 'attractive'.

senses.gloss: Attractive and pleasant to look at.
examples: She looked *fetching* in her new red coat.
What a *fetching* hat!
That's the most *fetching* photo of you I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Connected with the medieval system in which people worked land owned by a lord; also used of anything run in that old-fashioned, top-down way.
examples: Medieval Europe had a *feudal* system of lords and peasants.
The *feudal* lords owned most of the land.
The way that company treats its workers is almost *feudal*.

senses.gloss: Having a fever.
examples: The baby felt *feverish* last night.
If you're *feverish*, stay home from work.

senses.gloss: Very fast, excited and nervous.
examples: They worked at a *feverish* pace to finish on time.
The excitement grew more *feverish* as midnight approached.

senses.gloss: Using thin glass threads that carry information as light.
examples: Our town finally got *fiber-optic* internet.
Workers were laying *fiber-optic* cable along the highway.
*Fiber-optic* lines carry data much faster than copper wires.

senses.gloss: Made of or full of fibers.
examples: Celery is a crunchy, *fibrous* vegetable.
The scar was made of tough, *fibrous* tissue.
Older asparagus stalks are more *fibrous* and harder to chew.

senses.gloss: Often changing what one likes or who one is loyal to.
examples: Voters can be *fickle*.
He's a *fickle* friend who disappears when you need him.

senses.gloss: Of weather, luck or fame, changing suddenly and unpredictably.
examples: The weather in April is *fickle*.
Fame is the most *fickle* thing in show business.

contrast: *Fictional* is about stories: *a fictional character*. *Fictitious* is about something false, made up to fool people: *a fictitious name*.

senses.gloss: Existing only in a story, not in real life.
examples: Sherlock Holmes is a *fictional* detective.
The town in the movie is *fictional*.
All the characters in this book are *fictional*.

contrast: *Fictitious* means false and made up, often to deceive: *a fictitious address*. For characters in a story, *fictional* is the usual word.

senses.gloss: Invented and not true, often to fool people.
examples: He checked into the hotel under a *fictitious* name.
The company created *fictitious* invoices to hide the money.
The story he told the police turned out to be completely *fictitious*.

senses.gloss: Unable to keep still, always moving the hands or body.
examples: The kids got *fidgety* during the long ceremony.
He's a *fidgety* boy who can't sit still in class.
I get more *fidgety* when I drink too much coffee.

position: both — almost always before a noun

senses.gloss: In law and finance, involving a duty to manage money or property for someone else's benefit.
examples: Financial advisers have a *fiduciary* duty to act in their clients' best interest.
The board was accused of breaching its *fiduciary* responsibilities.
The relationship between a trustee and a beneficiary is *fiduciary*.

senses.gloss: Cruel, evil and cunning.
examples: The villain came up with a *fiendish* plan to rob the bank.
He gave a *fiendish* laugh.

senses.gloss: Extremely difficult or cleverly complicated.
examples: This week's crossword was *fiendish*.
It's the most *fiendish* puzzle I've ever tried.

senses.gloss: Angry, aggressive and ready to attack.
examples: The dog looked *fierce*, but it was actually friendly.
The tribe was known for its *fierce* warriors.

senses.gloss: Very strong or intense.
examples: Competition for the job was *fiercer* than we expected.
A *fierce* storm knocked out power across the state.
She is a *fierce* defender of free speech.

senses.gloss: Full of fire, or bright red or orange like fire.
examples: The plane went down in a *fiery* crash.
She has *fiery* red hair.

senses.gloss: Full of strong emotion, especially anger or passion.
examples: The senator gave a *fiery* speech.
Her brother has an even more *fiery* temper than she does.

senses.gloss: Of food, very hot and spicy.
examples: This salsa is *fiery*, so go easy on it.
He likes his wings with a *fiery* chili sauce.

contrast: Also an adverb: *We split the bill fifty-fifty*.

senses.gloss: Divided equally between two; with an equal chance either way.
examples: There's a *fifty-fifty* chance of rain tomorrow.
The two brothers have a *fifty-fifty* partnership.
The odds of winning are about *fifty-fifty*.

senses.gloss: Of words, used in a way different from their basic meaning to create an image.
examples: 'Break a leg' is a *figurative* expression.
I didn't mean it literally — it was *figurative*.
The poem is full of *figurative* language.

senses.gloss: Of art, showing people and things as they really look.
examples: The museum has a large collection of *figurative* paintings.
Her early work was *figurative*, but she later turned to abstract art.

contrast: Always capitalized. *A Fijian*, *Fijians* are nouns for the people.

senses.gloss: From or connected with Fiji.
examples: The *Fijian* rugby team is famous for its speed.
Our tour guide was *Fijian*.
We tried a *Fijian* raw fish dish called kokoda.

contrast: The country is *the Philippines* (with *Ph*), but the adjective and the people are *Filipino* (with *F*); *Filipina* is also used for a woman.

senses.gloss: From or connected with the Philippines.
examples: There's a great *Filipino* restaurant downtown.
My grandmother is *Filipino*.
Adobo is a classic *Filipino* dish.

senses.gloss: Connected with money and how it is managed.
examples: She works in the *financial* industry.
We're having some *financial* problems this year.
The reasons for closing the store were purely *financial*.

position: both — the 'all right' sense mostly after a verb: *I'm fine*
contrast: *I'm fine* means 'all right, nothing wrong', not 'wonderful'. *A fine* is a noun (штраф: *a parking fine*), and in speech *fine* is also an adverb: *The printer works fine*.

senses.gloss: All right, acceptable, or in good health.
examples: "How are you?" "I'm *fine*, thanks."
Tuesday is *fine* with me.
Don't worry — the car is *fine*.

senses.gloss: Of very high quality.
examples: The restaurant serves *fine* wines.
This is the *finest* chocolate in the country.
He did a *fine* job on the kitchen.

senses.gloss: Very thin or narrow.
examples: Her hair is very *fine* and hard to style.
Draw a *fine* line along the edge with a pencil.

senses.gloss: Made of very small pieces.
examples: The beach is covered in *fine* white sand.
Use the *finer* side of the grater for the cheese.

senses.gloss: Small and subtle, so hard to notice or understand.
examples: There's a *fine* line between confidence and arrogance.
The coach explained the *finer* points of the game.

senses.gloss: Of wood, stone or other material, having a smooth texture made of very small grains.
examples: Maple is a hard, *fine-grained* wood.
The sculptor chose a *fine-grained* white marble.

senses.gloss: Very detailed, dealing with small parts separately.
examples: The new app gives you more *fine-grained* control over your privacy settings.
We need a *fine-grained* analysis of the sales data.

senses.gloss: Very hard to please, especially about small details.
examples: My cat is a *finicky* eater.
He's *finicky* about how his coffee is made.

senses.gloss: Of a task or machine, needing a lot of care and attention to work.
examples: The old printer is *finicky* — you have to feed the paper by hand.
This is the most *finicky* recipe I've ever tried.

position: both — the 'ruined' sense only after a verb
takes: *with* + noun — done using or dealing with something

senses.gloss: Completed, or done with an activity.
examples: Are you *finished* with the scissors?
The *finished* house looks amazing.
Once the paint dries, the table will be *finished*.

senses.gloss: Ruined, with no hope of success or of continuing.
examples: After the scandal, his political career was *finished*.
If the bank says no, we're *finished*.

contrast: The opposite is pronounced differently: *finite* /ˈfaɪnaɪt/ FY-nyt, but *infinite* /ˈɪnfɪnət/ IN-fi-nuht.

senses.gloss: Having a limit or an end.
examples: The earth has a *finite* supply of oil.
Our time together is *finite*, so let's make the most of it.
There's only a *finite* number of tickets.

contrast: Always capitalized. *Finnish* is also the language (*She speaks Finnish*); the people are *Finns*. Do not confuse with *finish* (заканчивать).

senses.gloss: From or connected with Finland.
examples: Saunas are a big part of *Finnish* culture.
My coworker is *Finnish*.
She spent a winter in a *Finnish* village above the Arctic Circle.

contrast: *Fire-resistant* means hard to burn or slow to burn; *fireproof* means fire cannot damage it at all.

senses.gloss: Not burning easily, or protecting against fire for some time.
examples: Firefighters wear *fire-resistant* suits.
Brick is more *fire-resistant* than wood.
The new curtains in the school auditorium are *fire-resistant*.

contrast: Same meaning as *flame-retardant*. Without the hyphen it is often a noun: *Planes dropped fire retardant on the hills*.

senses.gloss: Treated with or made of a substance that slows the spread of fire.
examples: The theater curtains are *fire-retardant*.
Workers sprayed a *fire-retardant* coating on the wooden beams.
Crews used *fire-retardant* gel to protect homes near the wildfire.

senses.gloss: Not able to be damaged by fire.
examples: Keep your passports in a *fireproof* safe.
The walls between the apartments are *fireproof*.
She bought a small *fireproof* box for important documents.

contrast: *A firm* is also a noun — a company: *a law firm*.

senses.gloss: Fairly hard and not soft when pressed.
examples: I sleep better on a *firm* mattress.
Bake the cake until the top is *firm*.
Choose the *firmest* peaches for the pie.

senses.gloss: Strong and steady.
examples: He has a *firm* handshake.
Keep a *firm* grip on the rope.

senses.gloss: Strict and showing that you are in control.
examples: You need to be *firm* with the kids about bedtime.
She's *firm* but fair with her students.

senses.gloss: Definite and not likely to change.
examples: We don't have a *firm* date for the wedding yet.
She's a *firm* believer in hard work.
Is that a *firm* offer?

senses.gloss: Excellent, of the best quality.
examples: The hotel has a *first-rate* restaurant.
The service was *first-rate*.
She's a *first-rate* lawyer.

senses.gloss: In sports, belonging to the main team of best players, not the backups.
examples: He's the *first-string* quarterback this season.
The coach rested his *first-string* players in the fourth quarter.
She finally earned a *first-string* spot on the varsity team.

contrast: At American schools and colleges *freshman* is the traditional word; many colleges now prefer the neutral *first-year*: *a first-year student*.

senses.gloss: In the first year of study, work or operation.
examples: All *first-year* students live on campus.
She's a *first-year* teacher at a public school.
The *first-year* costs were higher than we expected.

contrast: Often a noun: *Their firstborn is starting college* (первенец).

senses.gloss: Born first in a family.
examples: Their *firstborn* son was born in May.
Emma was their *firstborn* child.
*Firstborn* children are often expected to be more responsible.

contrast: After a verb it is an adverb: *I saw it firsthand* (своими глазами).

senses.gloss: Coming from your own experience or from seeing something yourself.
examples: She has *firsthand* experience of running a small business.
We heard a *firsthand* account of the flood.
There's no substitute for *firsthand* knowledge.

contrast: *Fiscal* is about government money and taxes, or an organization's accounting year. For a person's money, use *financial*: *financial problems*, not *fiscal problems*.

senses.gloss: Connected with government money, taxes and spending, or with an organization's financial year.
examples: The company's *fiscal* year ends in June.
Congress is debating *fiscal* policy.
The city is facing a *fiscal* crisis.

senses.gloss: Informal: seeming dishonest or suspicious.
examples: Something *fishy* is going on here.
His story sounds *fishy* to me.
The deal got even *fishier* when he refused to show us the contract.

senses.gloss: Tasting or smelling of fish.
examples: The kitchen had a *fishy* smell.
This salmon tastes a little *fishy*.

senses.gloss: Starting and stopping, not steady or continuous.
examples: I had a *fitful* night's sleep before the exam.
Progress on the project has been *fitful*.
His sleep was even more *fitful* after the surgery.

senses.gloss: Made to follow the shape of the body or of the thing it covers.
examples: She wore a *fitted* black blazer.
Put the *fitted* sheet on first, then the flat one.
This shirt is more *fitted* at the waist.

contrast: *A fitting* is a noun: примерка (*a dress fitting*) or a small part (*pipe fittings*).

senses.gloss: Right or suitable for the situation.
examples: It was a *fitting* end to a great season.
It's *fitting* that she won the award in her hometown.
I can't think of a more *fitting* tribute to him.

position: both — the 'repaired' sense only after a verb

senses.gloss: Not changing; set at a particular amount or level.
examples: We pay a *fixed* rate on our mortgage.
The prices are *fixed*, so don't try to bargain.
Retirees on *fixed* incomes were hit hardest by inflation.

senses.gloss: Repaired and working again.
examples: Is the dishwasher *fixed* yet?
Once the brakes are *fixed*, you can drive it again.

senses.gloss: Attached in one place so that it cannot move.
examples: The camera stays in a *fixed* position.
The benches in the park are *fixed*, so you can't move them.

senses.gloss: Informal: arranged dishonestly so the result is decided in advance.
examples: Fans claimed the fight was *fixed*.
Nobody believed it was anything but a *fixed* election.

senses.gloss: Of a drink, full of small bubbles of gas.
examples: Kids love sweet *fizzy* drinks.
Do you want *fizzy* water or still?
This soda is *fizzier* than the one we had yesterday.

comparison: not gradable — an extreme adjective: *absolutely flabbergasted*

senses.gloss: Extremely surprised and shocked.
examples: I was *flabbergasted* when she said yes.
He looked absolutely *flabbergasted* by the news.
The *flabbergasted* crowd went silent.

senses.gloss: Of the body, soft and loose, with too much fat.
examples: He's gotten *flabby* since he stopped running.
My stomach is *flabbier* than it used to be.
She does push-ups to tone her *flabby* arms.

senses.gloss: Weak and not effective, with too much that is not needed.
examples: The essay is *flabby* and needs serious cutting.
The movie's *flabby* middle hour really drags.

contrast: Two pronunciations are heard in American English: FLAS-id /ˈflæsɪd/ and FLAK-sid /ˈflæksɪd/.

senses.gloss: Soft, weak and hanging loosely; also, lacking force or energy.
examples: The plants were *flaccid* from lack of water.
After a week of rest, his muscles felt *flaccid*.
Critics called the sequel even more *flaccid* than the original.

form: -ing from the verb *flag* ('to become weak or tired')
contrast: Nothing to do with *a flag* (флаг). After *be* it is the verb: *Our energy was flagging*.

senses.gloss: Becoming weaker, less active or less successful.
examples: The company is trying to revive its *flagging* sales.
A cup of coffee helped my *flagging* energy.
The ad campaign boosted the senator's *flagging* popularity.

contrast: Do not confuse with *fragrant* (ароматный) — one letter apart.

senses.gloss: Of something bad, done openly and shockingly, without trying to hide it.
examples: It was a *flagrant* violation of the rules.
The referee called a *flagrant* foul.
It's one of the most *flagrant* cases of fraud I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Breaking easily into small thin pieces.
examples: The croissants were warm and *flaky*.
Winter makes my skin dry and *flaky*.

senses.gloss: Informal: not reliable — forgetting plans, or working only some of the time.
examples: She's the *flakiest* person I know — she always cancels at the last minute.
Don't count on him; he's too *flaky*.
The Wi-Fi in this hotel is really *flaky*.

senses.gloss: Very confident, colorful and eager to be noticed.
examples: He's known for his *flamboyant* style.
The singer wore a *flamboyant* gold suit.
Her brother is even more *flamboyant* than she is.

senses.gloss: Made of or treated with a substance that makes it burn slowly.
examples: Children's pajamas must be made of *flame-retardant* fabric.
Some *flame-retardant* chemicals have been linked to health problems.
The seats on the plane are *flame-retardant*.

senses.gloss: Burning with flames.
examples: The chef poured brandy over the *flaming* pan.
Rioters threw *flaming* bottles at the police.

senses.gloss: Very bright red or orange, like fire.
examples: She has *flaming* red hair.
We watched the *flaming* orange sunset from the pier.

contrast: *Flammable* and *inflammable* mean the same thing — easy to burn; the *in-* is not 'not'. Americans use *flammable* on warning labels.

senses.gloss: Burning easily.
examples: Gasoline is highly *flammable*.
Keep *flammable* liquids away from the stove.
Some fabrics are more *flammable* than others.

senses.gloss: Bright, expensive-looking and designed to impress people.
examples: He drives a *flashy* red sports car.
Her outfit was a bit too *flashy* for the office.
The new phone is *flashier*, but the old one works better.

position: both — the 'unprepared' sense mostly in *catch someone flat-footed*

senses.gloss: Not ready for something that happens suddenly.
examples: The quick pass caught the defense *flat-footed*.
Officials were *flat-footed* when the storm hit.

senses.gloss: Having feet with a very low arch.
examples: He was *flat-footed* as a child and wore special shoes.
*Flat-footed* runners may need arch supports.

senses.gloss: Clumsy and without skill or imagination.
examples: The dialogue in the movie is clumsy and *flat-footed*.
It was the most *flat-footed* speech of the whole campaign.

senses.gloss: Pressed or made flat.
examples: We found a *flattened* soda can in the street.
The storm left the cornfields *flattened*.
The kids slid down the hill on a *flattened* cardboard box.

contrast: *Flattering* describes the words or the clothes; *flattered* is how you feel: *I was flattered by her comments*.

senses.gloss: Praising someone, often more than is true.
examples: The article about her was very *flattering*.
It's *flattering* to be asked to give the speech.

senses.gloss: Making someone look more attractive.
examples: That color is really *flattering* on you.
This haircut is much more *flattering* than your old one.

senses.gloss: Having a strong, pleasant taste.
examples: The soup was rich and *flavorful*.
Fresh herbs make the sauce more *flavorful*.
Heirloom tomatoes are the most *flavorful* ones at the market.

senses.gloss: Having little or no taste.
examples: The hospital food was bland and *flavorless*.
Supermarket tomatoes in winter are often *flavorless*.
The reheated rice was even more *flavorless* than before.

senses.gloss: Having a mistake or weakness that makes it less good or less correct.
examples: The study was *flawed* from the start.
It's a *flawed* but interesting movie.
His second argument was even more *flawed* than the first.

comparison: not gradable — an absolute adjective: *absolutely flawless*, *almost flawless*

senses.gloss: Perfect, with no mistakes or faults.
examples: Her performance was *flawless*.
He speaks *flawless* English.
The diamond is almost *flawless*.

contrast: Also a noun — a young bird learning to fly (птенец). As an adjective it goes only before a noun: *a fledgling business*.

senses.gloss: New and not yet experienced or fully developed.
examples: The *fledgling* company has only five employees.
After years of war, it was a *fledgling* democracy.
She runs a program that helps *fledgling* writers find agents.

senses.gloss: Lasting only a very short time.
examples: I caught a *fleeting* glimpse of him in the crowd.
Fame can be *fleeting*.
The good moods were getting more *fleeting* every week.

contrast: Always capitalized. *Flemish* is also the name of the Dutch spoken in northern Belgium.

senses.gloss: From or connected with Flanders, the northern part of Belgium.
examples: The museum has a whole room of *Flemish* paintings.
Antwerp is the largest *Flemish* city.
My neighbor's family is *Flemish*.

senses.gloss: Eating or destroying flesh.
examples: Piranhas have a reputation as *flesh-eating* fish.
Doctors treated him for a rare *flesh-eating* infection.
The movie is about a town overrun by *flesh-eating* zombies.

senses.gloss: Of plants and fruit, thick and soft.
examples: Aloe has thick, *fleshy* leaves.
Peaches and plums are soft, *fleshy* fruits.

senses.gloss: Of a person or body part, having a lot of flesh; slightly fat.
examples: He had a round, *fleshy* face.
The nurse gave the shot in the *fleshiest* part of my arm.

senses.gloss: Able to bend easily without breaking.
examples: The tube is made of *flexible* plastic.
Yoga keeps your body *flexible*.

senses.gloss: Able or willing to change to suit new situations.
examples: My job has *flexible* hours.
We're *flexible* about the date of the party.
Try to be more *flexible* with your plans.

contrast: After *be* it is the verb: *The lights are flickering*.

senses.gloss: Shining unsteadily, getting brighter and weaker again and again.
examples: We talked by the *flickering* candlelight.
The *flickering* light in the hallway gave me a headache.
A *flickering* hope remained that they would find him alive.

senses.gloss: Of birds and insects, not able to fly.
examples: Penguins are *flightless* birds.
The ostrich is the largest *flightless* bird in the world.
Over time, some island beetles became *flightless*.

senses.gloss: Changing plans or interests often; not serious or reliable.
examples: Her parents thought she was too *flighty* to hold a steady job.
He's charming but *flighty*.
She was the *flightiest* of the three sisters.

senses.gloss: Thin, light and easily broken or damaged.
examples: The tent was too *flimsy* for the wind.
She was shivering in a *flimsy* cotton dress.
Paper plates are *flimsier* than plastic ones.

senses.gloss: Of an excuse or evidence, weak and hard to believe.
examples: He gave a *flimsy* excuse for being late.
The evidence against her is *flimsy*.

senses.gloss: Not serious enough about something that deserves respect.
examples: Don't be *flippant* — this is serious.
He made a *flippant* remark about the accident.
Her tone was more *flippant* than she meant it to be.

senses.gloss: Behaving in a playful way that shows romantic interest.
examples: She gave him a *flirtatious* smile.
He's *flirtatious* with everyone at the office.
Their texts got more *flirtatious* over time.

contrast: After *be* it is the verb: *A leaf was floating on the water*.

senses.gloss: Resting on water or moving in the air.
examples: We had dinner at a *floating* restaurant on the river.
The lake was full of *floating* ice.

senses.gloss: Not fixed; able to change or move.
examples: Our company gives everyone one *floating* holiday a year.
The country switched to a *floating* exchange rate.

takes: *with* + noun — having too much of something

senses.gloss: Covered with water.
examples: Drivers should stay off *flooded* roads.
Our basement was *flooded* after the storm.

senses.gloss: Full of more things or people than can be dealt with.
examples: The market is *flooded* with cheap imports.
Her inbox was *flooded* with messages after the video went viral.

senses.gloss: Soft and hanging loosely.
examples: The puppy has big *floppy* ears.
She wore a *floppy* straw hat to the beach.
The lettuce gets *floppier* if you leave it out of the fridge.

senses.gloss: Made of flowers, decorated with flowers, or smelling like flowers.
examples: She wore a *floral* print dress.
The perfume has a light *floral* scent.
This white wine is fruity and *floral*.

position: both — in cooking after the noun: *eggs Florentine*
contrast: Always capitalized. In dish names it comes after the noun.

senses.gloss: From or connected with Florence, Italy.
examples: We spent the day admiring *Florentine* architecture.
The painter was *Florentine* by birth.

senses.gloss: Of a dish, made with spinach.
examples: I ordered eggs *Florentine* for brunch.
Chicken *Florentine* is served in a creamy spinach sauce.

senses.gloss: Too full of decoration or fancy words.
examples: The book is written in a *florid* style.
His speeches grew more *florid* with age.

senses.gloss: Of a face or skin, red.
examples: He had a *florid* face from years of drinking.
The old sea captain had a *florid* complexion.

contrast: After *be* it is usually the verb: *Business is flourishing*.

senses.gloss: Growing well, successful and active.
examples: The town has a *flourishing* arts scene.
They built a *flourishing* business from nothing.
Downtown seems more *flourishing* now than it was ten years ago.

senses.gloss: Decorated with a pattern of flowers.
examples: She wore a *flowered* dress to the picnic.
The old couch had faded *flowered* cushions.
The wallpaper in the guest room is *flowered*.

contrast: Also a noun: *the flowering of jazz* (расцвет).

senses.gloss: Of a plant, producing flowers.
examples: We planted *flowering* shrubs along the fence.
Dogwoods are popular *flowering* trees in the South.
Bees help pollinate *flowering* plants.

senses.gloss: Full of flowers, or smelling or looking like flowers.
examples: The tea has a sweet, *flowery* aroma.
She wore a *flowery* summer dress.

senses.gloss: Of language, using too many fancy words.
examples: Skip the *flowery* language and get to the point.
The second draft was even more *flowery* than the first.

senses.gloss: Of hair or clothes, long and hanging loosely.
examples: She had long, *flowing* hair.
The bride wore a *flowing* white gown.

senses.gloss: Smooth, graceful and continuous.
examples: He writes in a smooth, *flowing* style.
The dancer's movements were graceful and *flowing*.
Her handwriting became more *flowing* over the years.

contrast: After *be* it is the verb: *Prices have been fluctuating*.

senses.gloss: Going up and down or changing often.
examples: *Fluctuating* gas prices make it hard to plan a budget.
As a freelancer, she has a *fluctuating* income.
Patients with *fluctuating* blood pressure need close monitoring.

contrast: Say *fluent in English* or *speaks fluent English*. The adverb is *fluently*: *She speaks English fluently*.

senses.gloss: Able to speak a language easily and well.
examples: She's *fluent* in Russian and English.
He speaks *fluent* Japanese.
After a year abroad, my sister is more *fluent* than I am.

senses.gloss: Smooth and skillful, without stopping or making mistakes.
examples: By second grade, most kids are *fluent* readers.
He gave a *fluent*, confident presentation.

senses.gloss: Soft and light, covered with fur, hair or soft threads.
examples: The kitten is so soft and *fluffy*.
We bought big *fluffy* towels for the guest bathroom.

senses.gloss: Of food, light and full of air.
examples: Beat the eggs until they're light and *fluffy*.
These are the *fluffiest* pancakes I've ever had.

senses.gloss: Informal: light and not serious or important.
examples: The article was a *fluffy* piece about celebrity pets.
It's a fun but *fluffy* movie.

contrast: Very often a noun: *Drink plenty of fluids* (жидкость).

senses.gloss: Of a situation or plan, not settled and likely to change.
examples: The situation is still *fluid*, and we'll update you as we learn more.
Our plans for the trip remain *fluid*.

senses.gloss: Smooth and graceful.
examples: The dancer's movements were *fluid* and graceful.
His golf swing is more *fluid* than it was last season.

senses.gloss: Able to flow like a liquid.
examples: The lava stayed hot and *fluid* for hours.
Add a little water to keep the batter *fluid*.

contrast: Spelling trap: *fluor-*, not *flour-*.

senses.gloss: Of a light, produced by a glowing gas in a long tube.
examples: The office had harsh *fluorescent* lighting.
One of the *fluorescent* tubes in the garage keeps flickering.

senses.gloss: Of a color, extremely bright and seeming to glow.
examples: Road workers wear *fluorescent* orange vests.
She painted her nails *fluorescent* pink.

takes: *with* + noun — level with a surface, or having plenty of money
contrast: Usually a verb or noun: *flush the toilet* (смывать), *a flush of anger* (прилив).

senses.gloss: Exactly level with another surface.
examples: Make sure the shelf is *flush* with the wall.
The new cabinets are *flush* against the ceiling.

senses.gloss: Informal: having a lot of money.
examples: After selling the house, they were *flush* with cash.
Tech companies were *flush* that year and hiring fast.

senses.gloss: Of the face, red, from heat, illness, embarrassment or effort.
examples: Her face was *flushed* from the heat.
You look *flushed* — do you have a fever?
His face grew more *flushed* as the argument went on.

senses.gloss: Very excited and proud because of something.
examples: *Flushed* with victory, the team celebrated all night.
The candidate, *flushed* with success, thanked her supporters.

senses.gloss: Nervous and confused, often because of being rushed or embarrassed.
examples: She got *flustered* when the teacher called on her.
A *flustered* waiter dropped our plates.
He was more *flustered* than angry.

form: compound — phrase used as an adjective

senses.gloss: Of a business, dishonest or unreliable and likely to disappear quickly.
examples: Don't hire some *fly-by-night* contractor.
It turned out to be a *fly-by-night* operation.
Many of those online colleges were *fly-by-night*.

contrast: *Flying* is also a noun: *I hate flying* (полёты). *Pass with flying colors* means 'succeed easily'.

senses.gloss: Able to fly, or moving through the air.
examples: Mosquitoes and other *flying* insects come out at dusk.
Several people were hurt by *flying* glass.

senses.gloss: Fast and energetic, especially at the start.
examples: The team got off to a *flying* start.
He took a *flying* leap into the pool.

senses.gloss: Covered with or full of small bubbles.
examples: I like my latte hot and *foamy*.
The waves left *foamy* lines on the sand.
This soap is *foamier* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Central and most important.
examples: The fireplace is the *focal* point of the room.
Health care became the *focal* issue of the campaign.

senses.gloss: In optics, connected with the point where light rays meet.
examples: A lens with a longer *focal* length makes distant objects look closer.
Check the camera's *focal* range before you buy it.

contrast: American spelling has one *s*: *focused*, *focusing*.

senses.gloss: Giving all your attention to one thing.
examples: Stay *focused* — the test is almost over.
She's completely *focused* on her career right now.
I'm more *focused* in the morning than at night.

senses.gloss: Aimed clearly at a particular goal or area.
examples: We need a short, *focused* meeting, not a two-hour discussion.
The company is *focused* on small businesses.

contrast: *I don't have the foggiest (idea)* means 'I have no idea at all'.

senses.gloss: With a lot of fog.
examples: It was a cold, *foggy* morning.
San Francisco is *foggier* in summer than in fall.

senses.gloss: Unclear or confused.
examples: My memory of that night is a little *foggy*.
I always feel *foggy* after taking cold medicine.
I don't have the *foggiest* idea where he went.

contrast: For furniture the usual word is *folding*: *a folding chair*. *Foldable* is common for phones and gadgets, and after a verb: *The table is foldable*.

senses.gloss: Able to be folded to make it smaller.
examples: He just bought a *foldable* phone.
The table is *foldable*, so it fits in the closet.
A *foldable* bike fits easily in the trunk.

senses.gloss: Made so that it can be folded flat or into a smaller shape.
examples: Grab a few *folding* chairs from the garage.
We set up a *folding* table in the backyard.
He always carries a small *folding* knife.

senses.gloss: Friendly, simple and informal, in the style of ordinary country people.
examples: The governor is known for his *folksy* charm.
The café has a warm, *folksy* feel.
His speeches got *folksier* as the election got closer.

contrast: *Next week* counts from now; *the following week* counts from another time: *We arrived on Monday and left the following week*. *Following* is also a preposition meaning 'after': *following the meeting*.

senses.gloss: Coming next in time, after the one just mentioned.
examples: We met again the *following* week.
She moved to Denver the *following* year.

senses.gloss: About to be listed or shown.
examples: Please answer the *following* questions.
You'll need the *following* documents to apply.

senses.gloss: Taking stupid and unnecessary risks.
examples: It would be *foolhardy* to hike alone in this weather.
He made a *foolhardy* attempt to swim across the river.
Nothing was more *foolhardy* than driving through the flood.
